tools.name: mcp__Tamarind_Bio__updateMoleculeProperties
tools.description:
Add or change properties on molecules that already exist, e.g. wet-lab results for a group you
imported earlier: up to 200,000 rows in one call, nothing re-imported.

Each row names one molecule, by its moleculeId or by its name in groupId (names are unique in a
group), and carries the properties to write. Properties are MERGED: a key you send is added or
overwritten, keys you leave out are untouched, and an empty cell writes nothing. A value is stored
as a number when it plainly is one (the same rule as importMoleculeFile: 007, 1,234 and 12% stay
text), so searchMolecules filters and sorts on it and a benchmark reads
it as {"property": "<column>"} (or as a comparison's truth) on its next results read, with no rerun.
Tool scores can't be overwritten here. A value that doesn't fit a group schema's typed field comes
back in rejected with the reason (e.g. "field 'score' expects type float, got 'abc'").

Two sources; pass exactly one:
- fileName: a CSV/TSV uploaded with uploadFile (comma or tab detected). keyColumn is the column
  naming each molecule; a header of moleculeId / molecule_id / id is read as molecule ids, any other
  (e.g. name, design_id) as names in groupId. When omitted it is the id column if there is one,
  else `name`. Every other column is a property, or only `columns` when given.
    e.g. name,kd_nM,expression  ->  groupId=<group>, fileName="wetlab.csv"
- rows: inline, for a few hundred: [{"name": "ab1", "properties": {"kd_nM": 3.2}}, ...] or
  [{"moleculeId": "<id>", "properties": {...}}]. A property set to null is removed.

Limits per call: 200,000 rows, 2,000,000 values (rows x property columns), 500 property columns and
a 64 MiB file; split a bigger sheet by rows or pass `columns`. Rows are sent in batches of 5,000,
several at once; 100,000 rows take well under a minute. The
result counts molecules updated and rows not found, refused (with the reason, e.g. a key that is a
tool score) or ambiguous, and lists the first problems by row number. A batch that failed or did
not start in time is listed: call again with the same arguments and batches=[...] (sending a batch
twice writes the same values).

Args:
    groupId: The group the molecules are in. Required when rows name molecules by name; with it,
        only that group's molecules are written.
    fileName: The bare filename returned by uploadFile (.csv, .tsv or .txt).
    keyColumn: The file's column naming each molecule (see above).
    columns: Only these columns become properties (default: every column but the key).
    rows: Inline rows instead of a file.
    batches: Re-send only these batch numbers (an earlier result's failedBatches/notStartedBatches).

```ts
mcp__Tamarind_Bio__updateMoleculeProperties(args: {
// Batches
batches?: integer[] | null, // default: null
// Columns
columns?: string[] | null, // default: null
// Filename
fileName?: string | null, // default: null
// Groupid
groupId?: string | null, // default: null
// Keycolumn
keyColumn?: string | null, // default: null
// Rows
rows?: { [key: string]: any }[] | null, // default: null
}): Promise<// _WrappedResult
{
// Result
result: string,
}>;
```

tools.name: mcp__Tamarind_Bio__uploadFile
tools.description:
Upload a local file to your Tamarind file store (up to 5 GB).

UNDER 4 MB (a PDB, CIF, FASTA, small CSV): pass the bytes in `content` — no network
needed, nothing for a sandbox to block: uploadFile(filename="target.pdb", content=<text>).

LARGER (up to 5 GB) — call with just `filename` to get a
short-lived `uploadUrl` on mcp.tamarind.bio, then stream your file to it with
ONE shell command:

    curl -T /path/to/<filename> "<uploadUrl>"

The bytes stream through to your store; the curl prints a JSON result when
the file is stored. Afterwards the file
appears in getFiles(), the web Database tab, and can be referenced by its
BARE `filename` in submitJob/submitBatch file fields.

IF curl FAILS with HTTP 403 from a proxy (not from Tamarind), "could not resolve
host", "network unreachable" or HTTP 000, your MCP client's sandbox is blocking
outbound network — it is not an auth problem. The MCP tools
keep working (they go through the client, not your shell) — only the upload
curl needs egress to the uploadUrl's host (mcp.tamarind.bio in production).
The exact host to allow is named in the uploadUrl/instructions you get back;
tell the USER to allow that host, then re-run the curl:
  - Claude Desktop / Claude.ai: Settings -> Capabilities -> "Allow network
    egress" -> under "Additional allowed domains" add that host
  - Other MCP clients (e.g. Codex): add that host to the client's network /
    egress allowlist.

OVER 5 GB (e.g. sequencing FASTQ/BAM): do not use this tool. Run the
Tamarind CLI instead, which uploads up to 100 GB straight to storage in
resumable parts:

    tamarind files upload /path/to/<filename>

(install with `pipx install tamarind-cli` or `uv tool install tamarind-cli`).
The upload URL refuses a larger file up front with HTTP 413.

Orgs that store files in their OWN S3 bucket can't use this tool; it says so,
and the CLI or the web app uploads to the right bucket.

FALLBACK (no shell available, or a small file you can't enable egress for):
pass the file's bytes inline via `content` (text, or base64 for binary), up
to the 4 MB inline cap. The server writes them directly — no curl, no egress:

    uploadFile(filename="target.pdb", content=<file text>)
    uploadFile(filename="model.bcif", content=<base64>, encoding="base64")

FLAT FILES ONLY: pass a bare name like "target.pdb" (no "/").

Args:
    filename: Bare destination name, e.g. "target.pdb".
    content:  FALLBACK only — the file's bytes inline (no curl, up to 4 MB).
              Leave EMPTY to get an uploadUrl to stream to (recommended).
    encoding: "text" (default; for text like PDB/CIF/FASTA) or "base64"
              (for binary or non-UTF8 inline content).
    contentType: MIME type to store (optional).

Returns:
    JSON. Default: {"uploadUrl", "filename", "instructions", ...}.
    Inline fallback: {"success": true, "filename", "bytes", "hint"}.

```ts
mcp__Tamarind_Bio__uploadFile(args: {
// Content
content?: string, // default: ""
// Contenttype
contentType?: string, // default: "application/octet-stream"
// Encoding
encoding?: string, // default: "text"
// Filename
filename: string,
}): Promise<// _WrappedResult
{
// Result
result: string,
}>;
```

tools.name: mcp__Tamarind_Bio__validateBenchmark
mcp__Tamarind_Bio__validateJob
tools.description:
Validate job settings BEFORE submitting, so you can catch missing or invalid
fields and fix them (or ask the user) instead of submitting and surfacing a 400.

Pass the whole set in one call. `settings` takes a list of settings objects as
well as a single one. Every row is validated — nothing is sampled — so do not
sample, and do not call this tool once per job. If a list is too large for one
request, the answer says so and asks you to split it; split it then, keeping each
part as large as it will go.

Returns JSON. For a single settings object:
  { valid, normalized?, error?, ... }
For a list:
  { valid, count, valid_count,
    results: [ { index, valid, normalized?, error? }, ... ] }
`valid` is the aggregate — true only if EVERY row passed. `index` is the row's
position in the list you sent. HTTP 200 is used for both outcomes — read `valid`.

Read `results` to tell a bad row from a refused request: a list with one bad row
and a list refused as a whole (out of quota, a bad `jobNames`) both answer
`valid: false`, but only the first carries `results`.

IMPORTANT: only submit settings that came back valid:true WITHOUT a
`mutatedFields` warning. A mutated input means the validator silently dropped
disallowed characters (e.g. non-standard residues), so submitting as-is would run
the job on ALTERED input — fix the input and re-validate first. For a list this is
reported per row, and the aggregate `valid` is false if ANY row was mutated.

Then submit: one settings object with submitJob, a list with submitBatch in a
single call.

Args:
    type: Tool name — see getAvailableTools().
    settings: One settings object, or a list of them — see getJobSchema(jobType=type).
    jobName: Optional name for a single job. Pass it when you have one, so a
        collision with an existing job is reported now rather than at submit time.
    inputs: Protein Solubilization prepared pickerComplex references (one list per
        settings row for batches). Jobs checks their structure and ownership at submission.
    jobNames: Optional names for a list — same length and order as `settings`.
        A name repeated within the list is refused.

```ts
mcp__Tamarind_Bio__validateJob(args: {
// Inputs
inputs?: any[] | null, // default: null
// Jobname
jobName?: string | null, // default: null
// Jobnames
jobNames?: string[] | null, // default: null
// Settings
settings: { [key: string]: any } | { [key: string]: any }[],
// Type
type: string,
}): Promise<// _WrappedResult
{
// Result
result: string,
}>;
```

tools.name: mcp__Tamarind_Bio__validatePipeline
tools.description:
Validate a pipeline run WITHOUT executing or saving anything. ALWAYS call this
before submitPipeline — a pipeline run costs real compute, and most authoring
mistakes are caught here.

Takes the arguments submitPipeline validates: the graph (`pipeline` or
`templateId`+`version`), `bindings`, `settings` and `name`. submitPipeline's
remaining arguments — `runName`, `project`, `idempotencyKey` — name and tag the run
rather than describing it, and the validator does not read them, so passing them here
would change nothing.

If `validationUnavailable` comes back, the validator could not be reached and your
pipeline was NOT judged — retry a couple of times rather than editing the graph, and
if it fails identically every time, report it instead of looping.

Returns { valid, errors[] } at HTTP 200 for both outcomes; read `valid`. Each
error carries a stable `code`, the `node` it belongs to, the `field` at fault
where there is one, and a `message` telling you how to fix it. Codes you will
actually hit include `required-field-unset` (often a residue selection that
belongs in the binding, not in settings), `input-unbound`, `tool-unknown`,
`setting-invalid`, `param-out-of-range`, `chain-incompatible` and
`molecule-class-incompatible` (the upstream tool does not produce what the
downstream tool consumes).

`valid: true` is NOT a guarantee that submitPipeline will accept the run. Known
gaps, measured: it does not confirm the tools exist, and it does not check that a
bound molecule group exists or has anything in it. So if submitPipeline rejects a
graph this approved, believe submitPipeline — re-validating will not reproduce the
error, and the fix is in what it names (usually a tool name or a group id), not in
the graph's shape.

Fix the reported errors and re-validate until `valid` is true.

Args:
    name: A name for the pipeline/run. Required.
    bindings: One entry per input node, keyed by the input node's id. Give
        molecules exactly one way: {"group": "<groupId>"} for an existing
        molecule group, or raw values — {"sequences": [...]},
        {"smiles": [...]}, {"pdbs": ["<uploadedPath>"]}, {"sdfs": [...]} —
        and the server creates the group for you. A file input takes
        {"file": "<path>"}. Add "residuesByChain": {"A": "1-76"} where the
        template's residueFields ask for one, and "chainMapping" only when
        your chain IDs differ from the template's reference chains.
    pipeline: INLINE mode — a full pipeline IR. Call getPipelineSchema()
        first. Mutually exclusive with templateId.
    templateId: REFERENCE mode — an existing template to run.
    version: REFERENCE mode only — a version handle like "v2".
    settings: REFERENCE mode only — per-node overrides
        {nodeId: {settingKey: value}}, limited to the settings the template's
        author marked editable.

Returns:
    JSON: { valid: bool, errors: [{code, severity, node, field, message}] }.

```ts
mcp__Tamarind_Bio__validatePipeline(args: {
// Bindings
bindings: { [key: string]: any },
// Name
name: string,
// Pipeline
pipeline?: { [key: string]: any } | null, // default: null
// Settings
settings?: { [key: string]: any } | null, // default: null
// Templateid
templateId?: string | null, // default: null
// Version
version?: string | null, // default: null
}): Promise<// _WrappedResult
{
// Result
result: string,
}>;
```
